question: Assume today is 2026-08-25. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate total U.S. net electricity generation at utility-scale facilities (all sectors, all energy sources, excluding small-scale solar) in July 2026, in gigawatt-hours (GWh, equal to thousand megawatthours), as it will be first reported in the U.S. Energy Information Administration's Electric Power Monthly (Table 1.1).

target.what: Total U.S. net electricity generation at utility-scale facilities, all sectors and all energy sources, excluding small-scale solar (EIA Electric Power Monthly Table 1.1, 'Net Generation by Energy Source: Total (All Sectors)'), for the calendar month of July 2026
target.publisher: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Electric Power Monthly
target.cadence: Monthly; first published roughly two months after the reference month (preliminary), revised in subsequent months
target.caveats: Target period is completed relative to the 2026-08-25 cutoff but the first EPM report for July 2026 would not yet be published at cutoff, so the value must be estimated. 'Utility-scale' excludes small-scale/distributed solar (EIA's ~1 MW threshold); 'net generation' is gross minus plant parasitic lo

candidates.hypothesis: July 2026 utility-scale net generation will be close to the July values of recent years (2023-2025) adjusted for trend growth and weather; July is the seasonal peak month. The same-month prior-year values anchor the level and the year-over-year growth rate.
candidates.data_to_find: EIA EPM Table 1.1 monthly total net generation (all sectors) for July 2023, July 2024, July 2025, plus June 2026 and May 2026 if published before cutoff; also the 12-month trailing values to gauge trend. Minimum: July 2025 total and recent monthly YoY growth.
search_hints: EIA Electric Power Monthly Table 1.1 net generation July 2025
total net generation all sectors monthly GWh 2024 2025

candidates.perspective: EIA-930 hourly/grid monitor and weekly data
candidates.hypothesis: Lower-48 daily/hourly generation from EIA-930 (Hourly Electric Grid Monitor) aggregated over July 2026 gives a near-complete proxy for utility-scale net generation; summing daily totals and scaling for non-lower-48 (Alaska/Hawaii) gives the monthly total.
candidates.data_to_find: EIA-930 daily or hourly net generation totals for July 2026 (lower 48), or weekly generation estimates; the ratio of EIA-930 lower-48 total to EPM all-US total in a comparable month to bridge coverage. Minimum: July 2026 monthly sum from EIA-930 or a reliable weekly aggregate.
search_hints: EIA-930 hourly grid monitor July 2026 generation

candidates.hypothesis: Summing load (which tracks generation plus net imports) across major balancing authorities (PJM, MISO, ERCOT, CAISO, SPP, ISO-NE, NYISO, Southeast, etc.) for July 2026, then scaling to national total via each region's historical share of US generation, yields the target. Net imports are small relative to total generation.
candidates.data_to_find: July 2026 monthly load or generation by major ISO/RTO and the historical share of each region in total US utility-scale generation. Minimum: ERCOT, PJM, MISO, CAISO July 2026 totals plus their combined share of US generation.
search_hints: ISO peak demand July 2026 record heat

candidates.hypothesis: Total generation = installed utility-scale capacity by fuel × capacity factor × hours in July, summed across fuels. July capacity factors are high for gas and low for wind/solar relative to annual averages; using July-specific capacity factors and current capacity estimates constrains the total.
candidates.data_to_find: Utility-scale installed capacity by fuel (EIA-860M or preliminary 2026 capacity) and July capacity factors by fuel from prior years. Minimum: total utility-scale capacity mid-2026 and July blended capacity factor.
search_hints: monthly capacity factor July natural gas coal nuclear

candidates.hypothesis: July 2026 generation is strongly driven by cooling demand; a hotter-than-normal July raises generation above the seasonal baseline, a milder one lowers it. Degree-day anomalies and record peak-demand events in July 2026 indicate the direction and rough magnitude of deviation from the prior-year July.
candidates.data_to_find: July 2026 US population-weighted cooling degree days vs 30-year normal and vs July 2025; reported record peak loads in July 2026; NOAA/CPC climate data. Minimum: national CDD anomaly for July 2026 and any record-demand reports.
search_hints: July 2026 heat wave electricity demand record
US power demand July 2026 record peak

candidates.hypothesis: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook published before cutoff gives monthly or quarterly total generation forecasts for 2026 that can be used directly or as a cross-check; STEO forecasts are close to realized values at short horizons.
candidates.data_to_find: EIA STEO (July or August 2026 release) forecast of total electricity generation for Q3 2026 or July 2026, in TWh or GWh; any independent (e.g., analyst) monthly generation forecast. Minimum: STEO Q3 2026 total generation forecast.
search_hints: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook August 2026 electricity generation

candidates.hypothesis: Summing generation by fuel (natural gas, coal, nuclear, hydro, wind, solar utility-scale, other) for July 2026, each estimated from its own driver (gas prices/gas burn, nuclear outages, hydro conditions, wind/solar capacity), reconstructs the total and reveals which fuel drives deviation from prior July.
candidates.data_to_find: July 2026 generation or proxies by fuel: natural gas burn (EIA gas storage/consumption), nuclear outage schedules, coal stockpiles, hydro conditions, wind and solar capacity additions. Minimum: gas and coal generation estimates plus nuclear and renewables baselines.

candidates.hypothesis: July typically accounts for a stable share (~9-10%) of annual US utility-scale generation; applying that share to a 2026 annual total (from STEO or trend) yields the July estimate. The share is stable but shifts slightly with weather and renewables growth.
candidates.data_to_find: Historical July share of annual total net generation (2019-2025) and a 2026 annual generation estimate. Minimum: July share in recent years and 2026 annual total forecast.
search_hints: July share annual US electricity generation

assessment.note: All three are 2025 annual U.S. generation totals from EIA, but they differ in scope and vintage: p1 (4,430 TWh) is all-sector net generation, p32 (4,408 BkWh) is all-sector utility-scale from the November 2025 STEO table, and p38 (4,260 BkWh) is electric-power-sector only from the January 2026 STEO. They are not independent measurements; they share EIA's underlying survey/model. p1 and p32 are close and mutually consistent for all-sector scope; p38 is lower because it excludes industrial/commercial self-generation. Use p1/p32 for all-sector anchors and p38 only as a scope check.

Q3 totals from the same STEO table. p34/p35 are all-sector utility-scale Q3 2025/2024; p36/p37 are electric-power-sector Q3 2025/2024. The all-sector vs power-sector gap (~39 BkWh/quarter) is consistent across years, confirming the scope difference is stable. p34 is the best available anchor for a July-2025-scale level, but it is a quarterly total, so dividing by three assumes July is near the quarterly average — July is typically the seasonal peak, so this likely understates July somewhat.

Both are July YoY growth rates for all-sector utility-scale net generation (2023: +0.4%, 2024: +1.1%). They establish that recent July YoY growth has been modest and positive, supporting a low-single-digit growth assumption for July 2026 rather than a large jump. p56 also gives an absolute July 2023 level (425,655 GWh) in its quote, which is a useful level anchor.

p6 (May 2026 YoY +3.1%) and p29 (1H26 electric-power-sector generation +37 BkWh, +1.8% vs 1H25) both indicate 2026 generation is running above 2025. They differ in scope (p6 all-sector monthly, p29 power-sector half-year) and period, but both point to positive 2026 growth in the low-single digits. kept.name: 2026 annual utility-scale generation growth vs 2025

kept.name: July-to-quarterly-average ratio for Q3 generation
kept.rationale: July is typically the hottest month and slightly above the Q3 average (August is also hot but September cools). A small uplift over one-third of Q3 is appropriate; range allows July to be near or modestly above the quarterly average.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
